intro.heading: Running Benchmarks
intro.text:
The operational runbook for vt-bench.sh: prerequisites, enabling the probe, the thread-pool ceiling, how CONGA actually gets a config change onto the running JVM, and how to tweak JVM options beyond what CONGA renders (heap sizing, experimental/incubator flags).

For what the probe filter itself does and why it's a Servlet Filter, see the VT Bench Probe page.

prereqs.heading: Prerequisites
prereqs.text: One of the following load-testing tools, on your $PATH:

prereqs-example.code:
# wrk (preferred -- single process, Lua round-robin across URLs) apt install wrk # or: brew install wrk
# hey (fallback -- sequential per-URL, still fine for smaller runs) go install github.com/rakyll/hey@latest apt install hey

enable.heading: Enable the probe
enable.text:
Off by default -- this is a load-testing tool, not something to leave on in production:

http://localhost:8080/system/console/configMgr → "VT Bench Probe" → check Enabled
PID: org.motorbrot.vtbenchprobe.VtBenchProbeFilter

vt-bench.sh refuses to run silently against a disabled probe -- a disabled filter still returns HTTP 200 (the real page just renders), so the script checks for the X-VT-Bench-Thread response header first.

ceiling.heading: The thread-pool ceiling
ceiling.text:
httpThreadpoolMax (default 200 in local-plain.yaml) is the platform-thread ceiling. Virtual threads park on Thread.sleep; platform threads hold an OS thread for the duration of the sleep. Drive concurrency above the ceiling to see the difference:

httpVirtualThreads100ms I/O @ 500 concurrent
falsequeue fills, p99 spikes, RPS plateaus at the ceiling
truethroughput keeps scaling, p99 stays flat

conga-intro.heading: CONGA: how a config change actually reaches the JVM
conga-intro.text:
CONGA (devops/conga) is this repo's config-generation module: it takes a small per-environment YAML file (roles + tenants + a config: block of knobs) and renders it through Handlebars templates into the actual files each target consumes -- Traefik routers, webcache vhosts, Sling /etc/map mappings, and, for our purposes here, a plain text file of JVM system properties.

httpVirtualThreads and httpThreadpoolMax are knobs on the slingslop-runtime role. The role's template, devops/conga/src/main/templates/slingslop-runtime/http-java-opts.hbs, turns them into two -D flags (below). Nothing is hand-edited -- you change the YAML, CONGA regenerates the output file, and launcher/launch.sh picks it up automatically because it always reads whatever is currently at that path.

This is the SAME mechanism in every environment -- only the source YAML differs. Locally that's local-plain.yaml; in production it's prod-motorbrot.yaml (under the slingslop-runtime role config of the vps1 node). The Ansible slingslop role reads the exact same rendered http-java-opts file and appends it to the production JVM's launch options.

conga-yaml-example.code: nodes: - node: localhost roles: - role: slingslop-runtime variant: segment config: httpVirtualThreads: true # false = classic platform-thread pool httpThreadpoolMax: 200 # platform-thread ceiling (ignored when VT is on)

conga-apply-example.code: cd devops/conga && mvn generate-resources cd launcher && ./launch.sh

jvm-tuning-intro.heading: Tweaking JVM options (heap, experimental flags, ...)
jvm-tuning-intro.text: CONGA's http-java-opts only carries the two thread-pool flags above. Anything else -- heap sizing, GC tuning, incubator/preview features -- goes through launch.sh's EXTRA_JAVA_OPTS environment variable, which is concatenated into the final JAVA_OPTS alongside the CONGA-rendered flags (base flags + JDWP + EXTRA_JAVA_OPTS + http-java-opts, in that order).

jvm-tuning-heap.heading: Heap size example
jvm-tuning-heap.text: Give the launcher a fixed 512MB floor / 2GB ceiling, or cap it as a percentage of the container's memory limit instead of an absolute number:

jvm-tuning-heap-example.code:
EXTRA_JAVA_OPTS="-Xms512m -Xmx2g" ./launch.sh
# or, container-friendly (percentage of the cgroup memory limit instead of a fixed -Xmx): EXTRA_JAVA_OPTS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0" ./launch.sh

jvm-tuning-experimental.heading: Experimental / incubator flags
jvm-tuning-experimental.text: Incubating APIs -- like the Vector API (JEP 508) -- need an explicit module plus a preview-features unlock; genuinely experimental JVM flags need -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions before the JVM will accept them at all:

jvm-tuning-experimental-caveat.text: --enable-preview only helps code that was itself compiled with --enable-preview --release 25 (or matching --add-modules) -- it will not retroactively unlock preview behaviour in Sling's own bundles. This flag combination is only useful while experimenting with your own code that explicitly targets an incubating API, not as a general performance knob.

jvm-tuning-persist.heading: Making a flag permanent instead of ad-hoc
jvm-tuning-persist.text: EXTRA_JAVA_OPTS is one-off and easy to forget between runs. For a flag you want every teammate (and prod) to get automatically, add a new knob the same way httpVirtualThreads was added: a config: entry in the environment YAML, plus a line in http-java-opts.hbs that renders it.

jvm-tuning-persist-example.code:
# local-plain.yaml config: httpVirtualThreads: true httpThreadpoolMax: 200 maxRamPercentage: 75.0 # new knob
# http-java-opts.hbs -- append: # {{#if maxRamPercentage}} -XX:MaxRAMPercentage={{maxRamPercentage}}{{/if}}
